definition: A CPU register holding the address of the next instruction to execute. Each thread has its own, because each is at a different point in the code.
example: When the kernel switches threads it saves the old thread's program counter and loads the new one's.

definition: A tiny, extremely fast storage slot inside the CPU that holds a value the current instruction is working on. A thread's register contents are part of its private state and are saved and restored on every context switch.
example: An x86-64 CPU has 16 general-purpose 64-bit registers.

definition: Having several tasks in progress during the same period, so their steps interleave. They may take turns on one CPU or run at the same instant on several (which is parallelism).
example: One CPU switching between an editor and a download every few milliseconds runs them concurrently but not in parallel.

definition: Executing computations simultaneously on available hardware execution resources. Several physical cores can provide parallelism; simultaneous multithreading can also let hardware threads share a core’s execution resources.
example: Summing four quarters of an array on four cores at once is parallelism.

definition: Graphical user interface: windows, buttons and menus used to interact with a program. Keeping slow work off the event-handling thread can improve responsiveness; a separate thread does not by itself guarantee the interface never freezes.
example: A photo editor's GUI stays responsive while a worker thread applies a slow filter.

definition: An endpoint for communication that a program reads from and writes to like a file, usually for a network connection. The kernel delivers incoming data to it and sends outgoing data from it.
example: A web server holds one socket per connected client.

definition: Thread ID: on Linux, the kernel's identifier for one individual thread (task). It comes from the same number space as PIDs, and `gettid()` returns it.
example: The main thread of process 1234 has TID 1234; another thread might have TID 1240.

definition: A value that tells the scheduler how important a thread is compared with others. Depending on the policy it is a strict rank (real-time) or a weight affecting its CPU share (Linux nice).
example: An eligible real-time-priority-50 thread normally outranks fair-class work, subject to bandwidth controls and fair-server service.

definition: An operation that happens as one indivisible step from the point of view of other threads: no thread can see it half done. Atomic increments let threads share a counter without a lock.
example: C11's `atomic_fetch_add(&hits, 1)` adds 1 to `hits` atomically.

definition: A sequence that reads a value, computes a new one from it and writes it back. Unless the whole sequence is atomic or locked, another thread can slip in between and its update is lost.
example: `counter = counter + 1` is a read-modify-write sequence.

definition: A threading model in which every thread a program creates is its own kernel thread. Simple and able to use all cores; Linux (NPTL), Windows and macOS use it.
example: On Linux, 100 pthreads are 100 kernel tasks.

definition: A threading model in which all of a process's user threads run on a single kernel thread. Switching is very cheap, but the process can use only one core, and one blocking system call stops every thread.
example: A CPU-bound N:1 program on an 8-core machine runs no faster than a single thread.

definition: A threading model that multiplexes user-visible threads over kernel threads. Several kernel threads permit simultaneous execution; the number depends on the runtime, blocking calls, configured parallelism and workload.
example: Go multiplexes goroutines over OS threads; GOMAXPROCS limits simultaneous Go execution rather than the total OS-thread count.

definition: Next Generation POSIX Threading: an IBM-led M:N threads project for Linux in the early 2000s. It was abandoned once NPTL's simpler 1:1 design proved fast enough.
example: NGPT and NPTL competed around 2002; NPTL was merged into glibc.

definition: A Unix operating system originally from Sun Microsystems (now Oracle). It used the M:N threading model before Solaris 9 and then switched to 1:1.
example: Early Java "green threads" were developed on Solaris.

definition: The family of Unix calls that replaces the current process's program with a new one, keeping the same process ID. Usually called just after `fork()`.
example: `execve("/bin/ls", ...)` turns the calling process into `ls`.

definition: On Linux, the set of tasks that make up one process. Tasks created with `CLONE_THREAD` join their creator's thread group, and the group's ID is what user space calls the PID.
example: All 5 threads of process 1234 are in thread group 1234.

definition: Thread group ID: the identifier of a Linux thread group, equal to the TID of its first (main) thread. `getpid()` returns it.
example: In process 1234 the TGID is 1234 in every thread.

definition: The Linux system call that returns the calling thread's own thread ID (TID), as opposed to `getpid()`, which returns the thread group ID.
example: In a non-main thread of process 1234, `gettid()` might return 1240.

definition: A compiled programming language from Google, known for goroutines and channels for concurrency.
example: Go 1.25 made GOMAXPROCS respect container CPU limits by default.

definition: The Go setting that limits how many OS threads may execute Go code at the same time. Since Go 1.25 its default also considers cgroup CPU limits.
example: With GOMAXPROCS=4, at most four goroutines run Go code simultaneously.

definition: The part of the Go runtime that waits on many network sockets at once using epoll (on Linux), so a goroutine waiting for data needs no OS thread of its own.
example: Thousands of idle Go connections are parked on the netpoller.

definition: The Go mechanism for calling C code. A goroutine inside a cgo call occupies an OS thread, so heavy cgo use can raise a Go program's thread count.
example: Calling a C library from Go uses cgo.

definition: A lightweight Java thread (final in JDK 21) managed by the Java runtime and mounted on a small pool of OS "carrier" threads when it runs, the M:N model inside the JVM.
example: A Java server can run one virtual thread per request for tens of thousands of requests.

definition: An OS thread that executes a Java virtual thread while it is mounted. Many blocking operations unmount the virtual thread, freeing the carrier; pinning and some native or runtime operations can instead retain a carrier, depending on the JDK version.
example: JDK 21 can pin a virtual thread during certain synchronized or native operations; later JDKs changed some pinning cases.

definition: Java Development Kit: the Java compiler, runtime and libraries. Version numbers such as JDK 21 identify releases; 8u191 is an update of Java 8.
example: Virtual threads became final in JDK 21.

definition: A very cheap unit of concurrency in the Erlang language, managed by its virtual machine rather than the OS. Programs routinely run hundreds of thousands of them.
example: An Erlang chat server might run one process per connected user.

definition: Terminal programs that show live CPU and memory use per process; pressing H in `top` (or using `htop`) shows individual threads.
example: Running `top -H -p 1234` lists the threads of process 1234 by CPU use.

definition: Operating Systems: Three Easy Pieces, a free textbook by Remzi and Andrea Arpaci-Dusseau widely used for OS courses. Several lessons follow its presentation.
example: OSTEP's scheduling chapters introduce FCFS, SJF, RR and MLFQ.

definition: When a thread asks for something that is not ready yet (data, a lock, a timer) and the kernel puts it to sleep until it is. A blocked thread uses no CPU and cannot run.
example: A `read()` on a socket with no data blocks the calling thread until data arrives.

definition: The kernel's rule for how much virtual memory it promises to processes compared with the RAM and swap it has. Under strict policies, reserving more than the limit fails even if the memory is never touched.
example: With `vm.overcommit_memory=2`, Linux refuses allocations beyond the commit limit.

definition: Linux limits on how many threads can exist: `threads-max` is system-wide, `pid_max` caps the ID space, and `RLIMIT_NPROC` (`ulimit -u`) caps processes and threads per user.
example: `cat /proc/sys/kernel/threads-max` shows the system-wide thread limit.

definition: Small, fast hardware storage keeping copies of memory data or instructions. Cache levels and sharing vary by CPU; a miss at one level can be served by another cache, another core or main memory.
example: Inspect the machine’s cache topology rather than assuming every socket shares one L3 cache.

definition: The pthreads call that starts a new thread running a given function with one `void *` argument. It returns 0 on success or an error number such as `EAGAIN`.
example: `pthread_create(&t, NULL, work, &job)` runs `work(&job)` in a new thread.

definition: The pthreads call that waits for a thread to finish and collects its return value. Joining also frees the finished thread's resources.
example: `pthread_join(t, &result)` blocks until thread `t` ends.

definition: The pthreads call that marks a thread as detached, so its resources are freed automatically when it ends and nobody may join it.
example: A fire-and-forget logging thread is usually detached.

definition: The pthreads call that ends only the calling thread. Called at the end of `main`, it lets the other threads keep running instead of ending the process.
example: Ending `main` with `pthread_exit(NULL)` keeps worker threads alive.

definition: `pthread_t` is the type that identifies a pthread; `pthread_attr_t` holds optional creation settings such as stack size or detached state (NULL means defaults).
example: `pthread_t tid[4];` holds the IDs of four threads.

definition: A C pointer with no declared type, which can point to any object. pthreads passes one `void *` into a thread and gets one back, so you pass a pointer to a struct to carry several values.
example: A `struct job *` converts implicitly to `void *` when passed to `pthread_create`.

definition: A C type that groups several named fields into one object, laid out next to each other in memory.
example: `struct job { long sum; };` defines a struct with one field.

definition: An integer identifying a failure, such as EAGAIN or EBUSY. Many Unix calls report failure and set errno; pthread_create and pthread_join instead return an error number directly. Always check the particular API’s contract.
example: `strerror(EAGAIN)` gives "Resource temporarily unavailable".

definition: The C function that turns an error number into a readable message.
example: `strerror(rc)` turns the code returned by `pthread_create` into text.

definition: A slowdown where threads on different cores write different variables that happen to sit in the same cache line, so the line bounces between cores even though no data is actually shared.
example: Four per-thread counters packed into one 64-byte line can make a parallel loop slower than a serial one.

definition: The default state of a pthread: when it ends, its return value and resources are kept until another thread joins it. A joinable thread nobody joins leaks those resources.
example: Forgetting to join 10,000 finished joinable threads leaks 10,000 thread records.

definition: A thread whose resources are released automatically when it ends. It cannot be joined and its return value is lost.
example: `pthread_detach(pthread_self())` makes the calling thread detached.

definition: The function where a C program starts, run by the process's first (main) thread. Returning from it calls `exit()` and ends every thread.
example: `int main(void) { ... return 0; }` ends the process when it returns.

definition: The thread a process starts with, which runs main(). On Linux its thread ID equals the process ID. If it returns from main() the whole process ends; if it calls pthread_exit() instead, the other threads keep running.
example: In process 1234 the main thread has TID 1234; the threads it creates get other TIDs.

definition: A thread whose job is to repeatedly take work from a queue and do it, typically as part of a thread pool.
example: A server with 8 worker threads can process 8 requests at once.

definition: The queue of submitted jobs (tasks) waiting for a free worker. An unbounded queue can grow until memory runs out under overload; a bounded one rejects or slows submitters instead.
example: A bounded queue of 1,000 jobs rejects the 1,001st while all workers are busy.

definition: Java’s task-execution service interface, supporting submission, futures and orderly shutdown. Thread pools are common implementations, but an ExecutorService can use other strategies, including one virtual thread per task.
example: `Executors.newFixedThreadPool(8)` returns an ExecutorService with 8 workers.

definition: The Python standard-library module providing `ThreadPoolExecutor` and `ProcessPoolExecutor`: pools that run functions and return futures.
example: `from concurrent.futures import ThreadPoolExecutor`.

definition: Python's thread pool class. `max_workers` sets the pool size; since Python 3.13 the default is `min(32, (os.process_cpu_count() or 1) + 4)`.
example: With max_workers=10, at most ten pool jobs execute at once; idle workers are reused and fewer may be needed.

definition: Python’s executor using worker processes, so independent pure-Python jobs can run simultaneously on several CPUs. Arguments and results must be serialisable. Since Python 3.13 its default uses os.process_cpu_count(), which reflects affinity rather than a cgroup CPU quota; platform limits also apply.
example: `ProcessPoolExecutor(max_workers=8)` can keep 8 cores busy with pure-Python work.

definition: The parameter of Python's executors that sets the maximum number of worker threads or processes in the pool.
example: `ThreadPoolExecutor(max_workers=4)` never runs more than 4 tasks at once.

definition: An object standing for the result of work that may not have finished yet. Calling its `result()` method waits for the value.
example: `f = pool.submit(work); f.result()` waits for `work` to finish.

definition: In this module, one round in which every worker of a pool runs one job at the same time. With equal-length jobs, the number of waves is the job count divided by the worker count, rounded up.
example: Ten jobs on four workers take three waves: 4, 4, then 2.

definition: A rough guideline from experience, used as a starting point rather than an exact law and checked by measurement where it matters. Thread-pool sizing formulas are one example.
example: Start an I/O-bound pool at cores × (1 + wait / compute) threads, then measure.

definition: Python functions that report CPUs. `os.cpu_count()` returns the machine's logical CPUs; `os.process_cpu_count()` (3.13+) returns those this process may use under its affinity mask. Neither reads a cgroup `cpu.max` quota.
example: In a 2-CPU-quota container on a 64-CPU host, both can return 64.

definition: Global Interpreter Lock: in GIL-enabled CPython, a thread must hold its interpreter’s GIL to execute Python bytecode. Blocking I/O and many native operations release it. Isolated interpreters can have separate GILs, and free-threaded builds can run without one.
example: Two threads running a pure-Python loop take about as long as running it twice serially.

definition: The standard implementation of Python, written in C; the one you get from python.org.
example: `python3 --version` normally runs CPython.

definition: In CPython, how long a thread may hold the GIL before a waiting thread asks it to let go: 5 ms by default.
example: `sys.getswitchinterval()` returns 0.005 (seconds) by default.

definition: A Python module written in C (or similar) and compiled. It can release the GIL during long computations so other threads run meanwhile.
example: NumPy is largely a C extension.

definition: The standard Python library for fast arrays and numerical computing, implemented largely in C. Many of its long operations release the GIL.
example: A large NumPy matrix multiplication can run while other Python threads continue.

definition: Python standard-library modules for hashing (`hashlib`) and compression (`zlib`). Both release the GIL when working on large inputs.
example: `hashlib.sha256(big_bytes)` can run in parallel with other threads.

definition: Code is thread-safe if it behaves correctly when called from several threads at once, usually because it protects its shared state with locks or atomic operations.
example: Python's `queue.Queue` is thread-safe; a plain shared counter is not.

definition: Python's basic mutex. Use `with lock:` around code that reads and writes shared state.
example: `with lock: counter += 1` makes the increment safe.

definition: An optional CPython build supporting execution with the GIL disabled: experimental in 3.13 and supported from 3.14. Actual GIL state depends on startup settings and imported extensions; loading an incompatible extension can re-enable it.
example: The free-threaded interpreter is usually installed as `python3.14t`.

definition: Python Enhancement Proposal: a design document proposing a change to Python. PEP 703 made the GIL optional.
example: PEP 703 was accepted in 2023.

definition: The Python standard-library module for running code in separate processes, each with its own interpreter and GIL.
example: `multiprocessing.Pool(8)` spreads work over 8 processes.

definition: Python's way of serialising objects into bytes so they can be sent to another process. Process pools pickle every argument and result.
example: Sending a large ordinary array through a process pool can incur serialization and copying; shared-memory designs can avoid moving the full payload.

definition: An additional Python interpreter inside one process, with separate interpreter state. Python 3.14's InterpreterPoolExecutor uses isolated interpreters with their own GILs, enabling independent bytecode execution on several cores. Historically, not every subinterpreter configuration had a separate GIL.
example: An InterpreterPoolExecutor with 4 workers can run pure-Python code on 4 cores in one process.

definition: Python’s asynchronous-I/O framework using cooperative tasks on event loops. An event loop runs one task or callback at a time; other work runs when it returns or suspends. An await expression need not suspend if its result is already available.
example: `asyncio.run(main())` starts an event loop.

definition: A computation that can suspend and later resume. Calling an async Python function creates a coroutine object; a task drives its execution. Awaiting may suspend that task, but an immediately available result need not yield control.
example: `async def fetch(): await asyncio.sleep(1)` defines a coroutine.

definition: A Python expression that obtains a result from an awaitable. If obtaining it suspends the task, the event loop can run other work; an await that completes immediately need not yield control.
example: `data = await reader.read(100)` lets other coroutines run while waiting for data.

definition: A synchronisation point that makes a set number of threads wait until all of them have arrived, then releases them together.
example: `Barrier(2)` holds the first thread until a second one calls `wait()`.

definition: `cc` runs the system C compiler; `-O2` asks for standard optimisation and `-pthread` enables POSIX threads support for compiling and linking.
example: `cc -O2 -pthread sum.c` builds the parallel-sum example.

definition: The scheduler's list of runnable threads waiting for a CPU. Linux keeps one run queue per CPU.
example: In round robin, a preempted thread goes to the back of the ready queue.

definition: The fraction of time a CPU is busy running work rather than idle. For a SCHED_DEADLINE task, utilisation is the share of a CPU it reserves: runtime divided by period.
example: A CPU busy 900 ms in every second is at 90% utilisation.

definition: The time from a job arriving to it completing, waiting and running included.
example: A job arriving at 1 ms and finishing at 8 ms has a turnaround time of 7 ms.

definition: The total time a job spends ready in the queue but not running. For a job that never blocks, it is turnaround time minus its CPU burst.
example: A 3 ms job queued behind a 24 ms one waits 24 ms.

definition: Generally, how long a system takes to respond to a request. In scheduling it has a narrower meaning: the time from a job arriving to it first getting the CPU, which is what a user feels as lag in an interactive program.
example: Round robin with a 4 ms quantum gives three equal jobs response times of 0, 4 and 8 ms.

definition: A system, or kind of work, that runs jobs without anyone waiting interactively for them, so total throughput matters more than response time.
example: An overnight payroll run is batch work.

definition: A stretch of time a thread spends computing on the CPU before it blocks (for I/O, a lock or a timer) or finishes.
example: An editor might run a 0.2 ms CPU burst per keypress.

definition: A stretch of time a thread spends waiting for I/O (disk, network, keyboard, a lock) between CPU bursts.
example: A database query thread may compute for 1 ms then wait 10 ms in an I/O burst.

definition: Scheduling in which execution continues until the running task blocks, yields or finishes. A task that never cooperates can stall other work sharing that cooperative scheduler or event loop; it does not automatically stop independently scheduled OS threads.
example: Windows 3.1 and classic Mac OS used cooperative multitasking.

definition: Scheduling in which the kernel can take the CPU away from a running thread, typically on a timer interrupt or when a more urgent thread wakes. Every mainstream OS preempts user threads.
example: Linux can preempt a CPU-hogging thread within milliseconds so the editor responds.

definition: First-come, first-served: the scheduling policy that runs jobs in arrival order, each to completion. Simple and non-preemptive, but short jobs can wait behind long ones.
example: Bursts of 24, 3 and 3 ms in that order give an average wait of 17 ms under FCFS.

definition: A timeline diagram showing which job ran when, with time along the bottom. Used to work through scheduling examples by hand.
example: `| P1 | P2 |` over `0 24 27` shows P1 running 0–24 then P2 24–27.

definition: Under FCFS, short jobs queuing behind one long job, like cars behind a lorry. I/O-bound jobs pile up behind a CPU hog while devices sit idle.
example: Three 3 ms jobs behind one 100 ms job wait 100, 103 and 106 ms when all arrive together.

definition: Shortest job first selects the available job with the shortest next CPU burst. For independent known bursts arriving together on one CPU with zero switch cost, it minimises average waiting time. Unknown bursts require estimates, and repeated short arrivals can starve longer work.
example: Jobs of 6, 2 and 3 ms run in the order 2, 3, 6 under SJF.

definition: Shortest remaining time first: the preemptive form of SJF. When a new job arrives with less work than the running job has left, it takes over the CPU.
example: A 4 ms job arriving while a job has 7 ms left preempts it under SRTF.

definition: An average updated each step by blending the newest value with the previous average, so older values count for exponentially less. Schedulers can use it to predict the next CPU burst.
example: With weight 0.5, a guess of 10 ms and a burst of 6 ms give a new prediction of 8 ms.

definition: The scheduling policy that gives each ready job a fixed time quantum in turn, then preempts it and moves it to the back of the queue. Good response time and fairness; turnaround suffers when jobs are similar in length.
example: Three jobs with a 4 ms quantum run A, B, C, A, B, C... in 4 ms slices.

definition: Scheduling that always runs the highest-priority ready thread, with equal priorities usually sharing round robin. Low-priority work can starve if higher work keeps coming.
example: Under strict priority, a priority-10 thread never runs while a priority-20 thread is ready (where higher is more urgent).

definition: A static priority is set once by a user or administrator; a dynamic priority is adjusted by the OS as the thread runs, for example raised after it waits.
example: Windows gives a dynamic boost to a thread that has just finished waiting for I/O.

definition: In Linux's fair scheduler, a number that sets how big a share of the CPU a task gets compared with its competitors. Nice 0 is 1024 and each nice step changes it by about 1.25 times.
example: Weights 1024 and 820 split one CPU about 55.5% to 44.5%.

definition: The 1–99 priority of a Linux SCHED_FIFO or SCHED_RR thread, where higher numbers win within the RT class. Eligible RT work normally outranks fair work, subject to bandwidth limits and deadline-class fair-server service.
example: A SCHED_FIFO thread at priority 50 preempts one at priority 10.

definition: Gradually raising the priority of a thread the longer it waits, so that it eventually beats newcomers and starvation is prevented.
example: Improving one level per second, a thread at 127 matches priority 20 after 107 s.

definition: Multilevel feedback queue: a scheduler with several round-robin queues at different priorities. New jobs start at the top and are demoted when they use up their time allotment, so it learns which jobs are interactive without being told.
example: A CPU-bound job sinks to the bottom queue within its first few allotments.

definition: Compatible Time-Sharing System: an early time-sharing operating system built at MIT under Fernando Corbató, first demonstrated in 1961, in which the multilevel feedback queue was introduced.
example: CTSS let several users share one IBM computer interactively.

definition: Sharing one computer among many interactive users or programs by switching between them quickly, so each seems to have the machine to itself.
example: CTSS was one of the first time-sharing systems.

definition: The Association for Computing Machinery’s A.M. Turing Award recognises major contributions to computing. Fernando Corbató received the 1990 award for work on time-sharing systems.
example: Corbató won the 1990 Turing Award.

definition: In MLFQ, the total CPU time a job may use at one priority level, however many times it gives up the CPU, before it is demoted.
example: With a 10 ms allotment, five 2 ms bursts use it up.

definition: In MLFQ, periodically moving every job back to the top queue, so that low jobs do not starve and jobs whose behaviour has changed get re-evaluated.
example: Boosting every second gives a starved bottom-queue job a fresh start.

definition: Moving a job down to a lower-priority queue in MLFQ after it uses up its allotment at its current level.
example: A CPU-bound job is demoted from the 10 ms queue to the 20 ms queue.

definition: John Ousterhout's term, quoted in OSTEP, for a tuning parameter whose right value has no principled derivation, such as MLFQ's boost period.
example: Set the boost period too long and jobs starve; too short and interactive jobs lose their edge.

definition: FreeBSD's default scheduler. It estimates an interactivity score from how long a thread sleeps compared with how long it runs, and favours interactive threads.
example: A shell that mostly sleeps scores as interactive under ULE.

definition: A number computed from a thread's sleep and run times, used by schedulers such as FreeBSD's ULE to decide whether it is interactive.
example: A thread that sleeps 90% of the time gets a highly interactive score.

definition: A job that a person is waiting on, typically I/O-bound with short CPU bursts, such as an editor or shell. It needs good response time more than throughput.
example: A text editor thread wakes for each keypress and runs for well under a millisecond.

definition: A failure where a high-priority thread waits for a lock held by a low-priority thread, while medium-priority threads keep the low one from running. The high thread is effectively ranked below the medium ones, for an unbounded time.
example: Mars Pathfinder's resets in 1997 were caused by priority inversion.

definition: A NASA spacecraft that landed on Mars in 1997. Its repeated computer resets were traced to priority inversion and fixed by enabling priority inheritance.
example: Glenn Reeves, the flight software's cognizant (responsible) engineer at JPL, described the bug in 1997.

definition: A commercial real-time operating system from Wind River, used in spacecraft, aircraft and industrial systems, including Mars Pathfinder.
example: Pathfinder's inverted semaphore lived inside VxWorks' select/pipe code.

definition: A system call that waits until one of several file descriptors (pipes, sockets) is ready. In Pathfinder, the inversion involved a semaphore inside VxWorks' select and pipe handling.
example: `select()` can wait on a pipe and a socket at once.

definition: On Mars Pathfinder, the low-priority task that gathered atmospheric structure (ASI) and meteorology (MET) science data. It held the contended resource in the priority inversion.
example: The ASI/MET task ran rarely and at low priority.

definition: On Mars Pathfinder, the high-priority "distribution" task that collected the results of each cycle of transactions on the spacecraft's 1553 data bus and passed the data on to other tasks. It was blocked behind the low-priority ASI/MET task.
example: When bc_dist missed its deadline, bc_sched detected it and reset the computer.

definition: On Mars Pathfinder, the highest-priority "bus scheduler" task, which set up each cycle's transactions on the 1553 data bus. At the start of each cycle it checked that bc_dist had finished, and reset the computer when it had not.
example: bc_sched treated the missed deadline as a fault and reset the system.

definition: A locking protocol that raises a holder’s effective priority to that of higher-priority waiters so intermediate-priority work cannot keep delaying the holder. Boosts propagate along blocking chains; remaining boosts from other held locks may persist after one unlock.
example: With inheritance, a low thread holding H's lock runs at H's priority until it unlocks.

definition: A mutex priority-protection protocol that immediately runs a holder at the higher of its own priority and the highest ceiling of its held protected mutexes, even when nobody is waiting. POSIX PTHREAD_PRIO_PROTECT specifies this behaviour; ceilings must be assigned from intended thread usage. This differs from the original priority ceiling protocol’s additional system-ceiling admission rule.
example: A lock used by priority 10 and priority 50 threads gets ceiling 50.

definition: Priority inheritance passed along a chain: if a boosted lock holder is itself waiting on another lock, that lock's holder is boosted too, and so on.
example: H waits on L1 held by A; A waits on L2 held by B; transitive inheritance boosts both A and B.

definition: POSIX mutex protocol settings: `PTHREAD_PRIO_INHERIT` gives a mutex priority inheritance and `PTHREAD_PRIO_PROTECT` gives it a priority ceiling. They are set with `pthread_mutexattr_setprotocol`.
example: Real-time code usually creates its mutexes with PTHREAD_PRIO_INHERIT.

definition: The Linux kernel's priority-inheriting mutex, which handles chains of boosts. It underpins PI futexes and PREEMPT_RT sleeping locks.
example: Kernel docs describe the rt_mutex subsystem with PI support.

definition: The Linux real-time configuration, merged into mainline in 6.12, which makes almost all kernel code preemptible and turns most spinlocks into priority-inheriting sleeping locks.
example: Industrial controllers often run PREEMPT_RT kernels.

definition: A lock inside the Linux kernel that a waiting CPU busy-waits on (spins) instead of sleeping, used for very short critical sections. On PREEMPT_RT kernels most of them (spinlock_t) become sleeping, priority-inheriting locks; raw_spinlock_t stays a true spinning lock.
example: A driver protecting a small device register update with spin_lock() is using a kernel spinlock.

definition: The Linux command for setting a process's disk I/O scheduling priority, separate from its CPU nice value.
example: `ionice -c3 backup.sh` runs a backup only when the disk is otherwise idle.

definition: A per-process resource limit that lets an unprivileged process lower its nice value (raise its priority) down to a set bound.
example: With RLIMIT_NICE set to 30, a user may lower nice to −10.

definition: A count tracking references to an object. In CPython it participates in object lifetime management, alongside cycle collection; immortal objects and free-threaded implementations require additional rules. A simple increment/decrement model does not describe every object or guarantee immediate destruction.
example: For an ordinary non-immortal CPython object, adding a strong reference normally increases its reference count.

definition: Completely Fair Scheduler: Linux's normal-task scheduler from 2.6.23 (2007) until 6.6 (2023). It gives each task CPU in proportion to its weight by always running the task with the smallest vruntime.
example: Under CFS, two nice 0 CPU-bound tasks each get 50% of a CPU.

definition: Earliest Eligible Virtual Deadline First: the fair-class scheduler in Linux since 6.6, from a 1995 paper by Stoica and Abdel-Wahab. Among tasks that are owed CPU (eligible), it runs the one with the earliest virtual deadline.
example: For equally weighted eligible fresh requests starting at the same virtual runtime, a 1 ms slice has an earlier deadline than a 3 ms slice.

definition: Linux's scheduler from 2.6.0 (2003) to 2.6.23: per-CPU priority arrays let it pick the next task in constant time, with heuristics to guess which tasks were interactive.
example: The O(1) scheduler was replaced by CFS in 2007.

definition: A Linux scheduling class (merged in 6.12) that lets a scheduler written as a BPF program be loaded at run time and take over normal tasks.
example: Engineers can test a new scheduling policy with sched_ext without rebuilding the kernel.

definition: Rotating Staircase Deadline scheduler: Con Kolivas's 2007 fairness-based scheduler patches for Linux, which showed a simpler fair approach worked and prompted CFS.
example: RSDL was never merged, but CFS followed soon after.

definition: One level in Linux’s scheduler hierarchy, such as deadline, real-time, fair or idle. Higher eligible classes normally take precedence, subject to bandwidth limits. A deadline-class fair server can dispatch fair work even while RT work is runnable.
example: An unthrottled FIFO task normally outranks fair work, with fair-server service as a separate qualification.

definition: In Linux, the per-thread setting that chooses a scheduling class and its rules: SCHED_NORMAL, SCHED_BATCH, SCHED_IDLE, SCHED_FIFO, SCHED_RR or SCHED_DEADLINE.
example: `chrt -p <pid>` prints a thread's scheduling policy.

definition: The default Linux policy for ordinary threads, scheduled by the fair class (CFS/EEVDF) according to nice values. User space calls it SCHED_OTHER.
example: A newly started program runs under SCHED_NORMAL at nice 0.

definition: A Linux fair-class policy for non-interactive work that retains nice-based proportional sharing while adjusting wake-up treatment. It is a policy hint, not a fixed long time slice or a universal promise of fewer preemptions.
example: `chrt -b 0 ./build` runs a build under SCHED_BATCH.

definition: A fair-class Linux policy with an extremely low weight, for background work. It still gets a small share; it is not the per-CPU idle task.
example: A low-importance indexer can run under SCHED_IDLE.

definition: A Linux real-time policy with no round-robin time slice. It normally continues until blocking, yielding or preemption by higher-priority or higher-class work; bandwidth throttling and fair-server service also qualify this. ps displays FF.
example: `chrt -f 50 ./audio-engine` runs a program under SCHED_FIFO priority 50.

definition: A Linux real-time policy like SCHED_FIFO, except that threads of equal priority take turns with a time slice (100 ms by default, `sched_rr_timeslice_ms`).
example: Two SCHED_RR threads at priority 20 alternate every 100 ms.

definition: Linux's top scheduling policy (since 3.14). A task declares a runtime, deadline and period instead of a priority; the kernel admits it only if the CPU time fits, then schedules by earliest deadline first.
example: 5 ms of runtime every 16.7 ms frame is a typical SCHED_DEADLINE reservation.

definition: A deadline-class reservation (Linux 6.12) that guarantees fair-class tasks some CPU even while real-time tasks are busy.
example: A runaway SCHED_FIFO thread no longer starves the shell completely when the fair server is active.

definition: A Linux safety limit on how much CPU real-time tasks may use: by default 950,000 µs in every 1,000,000 µs (95%), leaving the rest for others.
example: `cat /proc/sys/kernel/sched_rt_runtime_us` normally prints 950000.

definition: The kernel deliberately holding back work that has used up an allowance. For CPU, a cgroup that has spent its quota for the period (or real-time tasks that hit the real-time limit) is stopped from running until the next period; memory and I/O controllers throttle in their own ways.
example: A container that uses its 200 ms quota in 25 ms is throttled for the other 75 ms of the period.

definition: The Linux mechanism that caps how much CPU time a cgroup's tasks may use per period (`cpu.max`), throttling the group when it runs out.
example: `cpu.max = 50000 100000` limits a group to half a CPU.

definition: The fair scheduler's imaginary reference that serves runnable competitors simultaneously in proportion to their scheduling weights. Equal weights give equal shares; unequal weights do not.
example: With 4 tasks, the ideal CPU would run each at a quarter speed simultaneously.

definition: CPU execution time scaled by scheduling weight and tracked in nanoseconds by Linux’s fair class. Nice 0 advances at the reference rate; higher-weight tasks advance more slowly. Classic CFS selects the smallest vruntime; EEVDF also requires eligibility and virtual-deadline comparison.
example: A nice 5 task running 6 ms gains about 18.3 ms of vruntime.

definition: A self-balancing binary search tree that keeps itself roughly balanced, so finding, inserting and removing take O(log n) time for n items. CFS keeps runnable tasks in one, ordered by vruntime.
example: A balanced tree keeps path lengths logarithmic in its number of nodes; the exact comparisons and rotations depend on its shape and operation.

definition: In a binary search tree, the node with the smallest key, reached by repeatedly following left children. Classic CFS caches this node for fast smallest-vruntime selection. The rightmost node is the opposite extreme, not an alias.
example: In a tree of vruntimes 10, 25, 40 and 70, the leftmost node holds 10.

definition: The scale of scheduling time decisions. Classic CFS used minimum-granularity tunables to avoid excessively short service slices; exact preemption rules and tunables depend on kernel version and scheduling policy.
example: CFS's default minimum granularity was 0.75 ms, scaled up on bigger machines.

definition: A set of tasks the fair scheduler treats as one unit when dividing CPU between groups (set up by cgroups or autogroup). Shares by weight apply within one group.
example: Two terminal sessions under autogroup are two fair groups.

definition: A monotonic per-run-queue virtual-runtime reference in Linux's fair scheduler. Classic CFS places sleepers relative to it; EEVDF adds lag-aware placement. It is maintained as a floor from tracked entities rather than always equalling the smallest current queued value.
example: A task waking after a minute is moved up to near min_vruntime rather than keeping its old tiny vruntime.

definition: A task that has been blocked (asleep) and becomes runnable again. Fair schedulers must stop sleepers from claiming all the CPU they "missed".
example: An editor that slept for a minute is a sleeper when the next key arrives.

definition: A target for service timing. In classic CFS, it was the scheduling period aimed at giving runnable tasks service, extended when minimum granularity required it. Historical defaults used 6 ms before CPU-count scaling; this is not an application-response guarantee.
example: With 4 runnable tasks and a 24 ms target latency, each got about 6 ms per round.

definition: Classic CFS's minimum-granularity target used when choosing scheduling periods and service slices. It helps avoid excessively small slices as runnable task counts grow; weights and other preemption conditions still affect actual execution.
example: CFS's 0.75 ms minimum, scaled ×4 on 8 CPUs, is 3 ms.

definition: Ion Stoica and Hussein Abdel-Wahab, whose 1995 technical report described the EEVDF algorithm that Linux adopted in 6.6.
example: Linux's EEVDF implementation cites their 1995 paper.

definition: In EEVDF, the difference between the CPU service a task would have received on the ideal CPU and what it actually got. Positive lag means it is owed CPU; negative means it has had more than its share.
example: A task whose vruntime is below the queue average has positive lag.

definition: In EEVDF, a task is eligible when its lag is zero or positive, meaning its vruntime is at or below the queue's weighted average. Only eligible tasks may be picked.
example: With an average vruntime of 10, tasks at 8 and 10 are eligible and one at 12 is not.

definition: In EEVDF, a task's vruntime plus its requested slice scaled by its weight. Among eligible tasks, the one with the earliest virtual deadline runs next.
example: A fresh nice 0 request starting at virtual runtime 10 ms with a 0.5 ms slice has virtual deadline 10.5 ms.

definition: An average in which each value counts in proportion to a weight. EEVDF averages tasks' vruntimes weighted by their scheduling weights.
example: Weights 3 and 1 on values 10 and 20 give (30 + 20) / 4 = 12.5.

definition: The default service request used by EEVDF when a task has no custom slice. In reviewed Linux 6.12 source it is 0.75 ms before default logarithmic CPU-count scaling, reaching 3 ms at eight or more CPUs. Settings and later kernels can differ.
example: For equal starting virtual runtimes and fresh requests, a nice 0 task's 1 ms slice has an earlier deadline than a 3 ms request.

definition: The Linux system call that sets a thread's scheduling policy and parameters, including SCHED_DEADLINE runtime/deadline/period and (since 6.12) a fair task's custom slice in `sched_runtime`.
example: `sched_setattr()` fails with EBUSY when a deadline reservation does not fit.

definition: An EEVDF technique introduced in Linux 6.12 that can keep an over-served sleeping task represented on the run queue until negative lag decays. The sleeping task is not thereby runnable; this prevents brief sleeps erasing its service debt.
example: A task 2 ms ahead of its share that sleeps briefly is not put back as if its debt had been cleared.

definition: The Linux source file implementing the fair scheduling class, CFS and now EEVDF.
example: The vruntime update code lives in kernel/sched/fair.c.

definition: Hierarchical fair scheduling that divides contended CPU service among sibling task groups by group weight, then among their members. Groups can be nested beyond two levels; quotas and topology also constrain service.
example: A 16-thread process alone in its group gets the same share as a 1-thread process in another equal-weight group.

definition: The cgroup v2 file holding a group's CPU weight (1 to 10,000, default 100). It only matters when groups compete; an uncontested group can use idle CPUs freely. cgroup v1's equivalent was cpu.shares (default 1024).
example: A weight-10 and a weight-100 group split a busy CPU about 9% to 91%.

definition: A Linux feature (since 2.6.38) that automatically puts each terminal session in its own scheduling group, so a big build in one terminal does not swamp the desktop.
example: With autogroup, `make -j32` in one terminal and a video player in another get about half the CPU each.

definition: A group of processes started from one login or terminal, identified by a session ID. Autogroup makes one scheduling group per session.
example: Opening a new terminal window starts a new session.

definition: Runs the `make` build tool with up to 32 compile jobs at once, keeping many CPUs busy.
example: `make -j32` on a 32-CPU machine compiles 32 files in parallel.

definition: Happening as events occur, with only a short delay. In scheduling and embedded systems it has a stricter meaning: computing where results must arrive within deadlines, not just eventually (audio, industrial control, trading). Linux's RT classes give such threads strict priority over normal work.
example: An audio thread must fill each buffer within a few milliseconds or the sound clicks.

definition: CAP_SYS_NICE is the Linux capability allowing a process to raise priorities and set real-time policies; RLIMIT_RTPRIO lets an unprivileged process use real-time priorities up to a limit.
example: A process without CAP_SYS_NICE or RLIMIT_RTPRIO cannot switch itself to SCHED_FIFO.

definition: The Linux command for viewing or setting a process's real-time scheduling policy and priority (`-f` FIFO, `-r` round robin, `-d` deadline, `-p` inspect a PID).
example: `chrt -f 50 ./audio-engine` runs the program under SCHED_FIFO priority 50.

definition: A loop that keeps running on the CPU without blocking or yielding, for example repeatedly checking a condition.
example: A real-time thread stuck in a busy loop starves everything below it on that CPU.

definition: Earliest Deadline First selects the ready job with the earliest absolute deadline. On one ideal preemptive CPU, independent periodic tasks with deadlines equal to periods are schedulable when total worst-case utilisation is at most one; blocking, overhead, different deadlines and multiprocessors require additional analysis.
example: SCHED_DEADLINE dispatches tasks by EDF.

definition: The algorithm SCHED_DEADLINE uses to enforce each task's reservation: a task that tries to run longer than its runtime in a period is held back until its next period.
example: A deadline task reserving 5 ms per 16.7 ms is stopped after 5 ms even if it wants more.

definition: Checking a new request against the capacity already promised, and refusing it up front if accepting it would overcommit the system, rather than letting everything degrade later. Linux's SCHED_DEADLINE does this for CPU reservations: a new task is refused if the total reserved bandwidth would exceed the limit.
example: Three deadline tasks reserving 30%, 40% and 30% of one CPU fail admission against a 95% limit.

definition: An error code meaning "device or resource busy". `sched_setattr()` returns it when a SCHED_DEADLINE reservation fails admission control.
example: Requesting more deadline bandwidth than is free gives EBUSY.

definition: The longest time a piece of code can take to run on given hardware. Real-time guarantees depend on knowing it; a deadline reservation smaller than it can be missed.
example: If a render step can take up to 6 ms, a 5 ms runtime reservation is too small.

definition: A test proving that a set of real-time tasks will always meet their deadlines under a given scheduler. It is stricter than a simple utilisation check.
example: Utilisation at most 100% is a schedulability test for EDF on one CPU with deadlines equal to periods.

definition: In Linux, a set of CPUs that share real-time and deadline admission accounting. By default all CPUs form one root domain.
example: An eight-CPU root domain with a configured 95% total deadline-bandwidth limit has 7.6 CPUs of reservation capacity before accounting for fair-server reservations.

definition: Scheduling-class codes in the `ps` CLS column: TS for the fair class (time sharing), FF for SCHED_FIFO, RR for SCHED_RR, DLN for SCHED_DEADLINE.
example: `ps -eLo cls,comm` shows TS for most programs.

definition: The priority column in `top`. For normal tasks it is 20 plus the nice value; real-time tasks show negative numbers (minus 1 minus their real-time priority), and `rt` at real-time priority 99.
example: A nice 0 task shows PR 20 in top.

definition: A Linux filesystem exposing kernel debugging interfaces, usually mounted at /sys/kernel/debug. Several fair-scheduler debug tunables moved there in Linux 5.13; other scheduling controls remain sysctls and access depends on configuration and permissions.
example: `ls /sys/kernel/debug/sched/` lists the scheduler's debug tunables.

definition: A kernel setting an administrator can change at run time, usually through a file in /proc or /sys.
example: `sched_rr_timeslice_ms` is a scheduler tunable.

definition: The physical slot on a motherboard holding one CPU chip; a multi-socket server has several chips, each usually its own NUMA node.
example: A two-socket server with 32-core chips has 64 cores.

definition: One of several smaller dies packaged together to make a CPU. Cores on the same chiplet usually share a last-level cache.
example: AMD EPYC processors are built from several core chiplets.

definition: Non-uniform memory access: memory-access cost depends on the relationship between a CPU and the memory node holding a page. Nodes need not map one-to-one to sockets; topology and workload determine the local/remote cost.
example: On a two-socket server, a thread on node 1 reading node 0's memory crosses the interconnect.

definition: A locality domain for memory allocation and CPU access. A NUMA node may contain CPUs, memory or both; memoryless and CPU-less nodes exist. Relative access cost depends on the hardware topology.
example: `numactl --hardware` lists each node's CPUs and memory.

definition: The final hardware cache level before accesses proceed beyond the cache hierarchy. It is often an L3 shared by a group of cores, but level, size and sharing vary by CPU design.
example: Waking a thread on a CPU sharing its last-level cache keeps much of its data warm.

definition: Dynamic random-access memory: the main memory chips of a computer. Much larger but slower than CPU caches.
example: A server may have 512 GB of DRAM split across its NUMA nodes.

definition: The link between CPU sockets (or chiplets) that carries remote memory accesses and cache-coherence traffic, slower than local access.
example: Intel's UPI and AMD's Infinity Fabric are CPU interconnects.

definition: A scheduling design with a queue for each CPU rather than one global queue. Per-queue locking reduces shared contention and helps locality; migration and wake-up placement must address imbalance.
example: Linux has used per-CPU run queues since 2.6.0.

definition: One CPU having more runnable work than another, so some work waits while a CPU sits idle.
example: CPU 0 with four runnable threads while CPU 1 is idle is a load imbalance.

definition: Moving a task between CPUs or run queues. This can balance runnable work but may disturb cache or NUMA locality. Moving physical memory pages between nodes is page migration, a related but different operation.
example: The balancer migrates a thread from a busy CPU to an idle one.

definition: A balancing technique in which an idle or lightly loaded worker pulls tasks from a busier worker's queue.
example: Go's scheduler lets an idle processor steal goroutines from another's queue.

definition: Java's work-stealing thread pool, used for recursive parallel tasks and as the default carrier pool for virtual threads.
example: Java parallel streams run on the common ForkJoinPool.

definition: An asynchronous runtime for Rust. Its multi-threaded scheduler uses worker queues and work stealing; a separate current-thread runtime runs tasks on its calling thread.
example: A Rust web server built on Tokio runs many async tasks on a few threads.

definition: The Linux scheduler moving tasks between CPUs' run queues to even out work: periodically from the scheduler tick, when a CPU is about to go idle ("newidle"), and when choosing a CPU for a waking task.
example: When CPU 5 has nothing to run, newidle balancing pulls a task from busy CPU 2.

definition: A level in Linux's description of the CPU topology (SMT siblings, cores sharing a cache, NUMA nodes) over which load balancing happens, more eagerly at lower levels.
example: Balancing within an SMT domain happens often; across NUMA domains, rarely.

definition: Choosing which CPU a thread runs on when it wakes: Linux prefers its previous CPU or an idle one sharing its last-level cache, and may place it near the thread that woke it (the waker).
example: A thread woken by a network interrupt may be placed on an idle CPU sharing the same L3.

definition: A Linux tunable (0.5 ms by default) below which a task that ran recently counts as cache-hot, so the balancer prefers not to move it.
example: A task that ran 0.2 ms ago may be treated as cache-hot under the checked 0.5 ms threshold; other migration conditions still matter.

definition: Per-entity load tracking: Linux's running, decaying averages of each task's and CPU's load, runnable time and utilisation, used by the load balancer and frequency scaling.
example: A task busy half the time settles near 50% PELT utilisation.

definition: Another logical CPU sharing one physical core through simultaneous multithreading. Siblings share some execution and cache resources; whether co-running jobs gain throughput or suffer contention depends on the hardware and workload.
example: On a CPU where 0/1 are siblings, `taskset -c 0,1` puts two threads on one core.

definition: Restricting a thread to particular CPUs with a hard affinity mask, so the balancer can no longer move it elsewhere.
example: Pinning restricts this thread; separately exclude competing work and inspect SMT siblings when seeking a dedicated core.

definition: The Linux system call (and Python `os` wrapper) that sets a thread's CPU affinity mask; `sched_getaffinity` reads it. `pthread_setaffinity_np` does the same for a given pthread. The mask is inherited across fork().
example: `os.sched_setaffinity(0, {2, 3})` limits the calling thread to CPUs 2 and 3.

definition: A cgroup controller that restricts a whole group of processes to chosen CPUs (`cpuset.cpus`) and memory nodes (`cpuset.mems`). Processes inside cannot widen it.
example: A container given `cpuset.cpus = 4-7` can only run on CPUs 4 to 7.

definition: The smallest unit Kubernetes runs: one or more containers scheduled together on one machine, sharing network and resource settings.
example: A pod with a 2-CPU limit gets `cpu.max = 200000 100000`.

definition: A Kubernetes kubelet policy that gives containers in Guaranteed pods (requests equal to limits) with whole-number CPU requests exclusive logical CPUs. The `full-pcpus-only` option makes it allocate whole physical cores.
example: A Guaranteed container requesting 4 CPUs gets 4 logical CPUs no other container uses.

definition: A Kubernetes CPU reservation used for placement and for proportional CPU sharing under contention. It maps to cgroup CPU shares or weight; it is not a hard CPU cap, nor a promise that every workload always receives that throughput.
example: A 500m CPU request contributes a half-CPU reservation for placement and proportional shares under contention; achieved service depends on the competing hierarchy and capacity.

definition: A Kubernetes CPU limit normally enforced through cgroup bandwidth quota, causing throttling when that budget is exhausted. The accounting period is commonly 100 ms but is configurable; ancestor limits and CPU-manager configuration can also matter.
example: A 2-CPU limit allows 200 ms of CPU time per 100 ms period.

definition: High-frequency trading: automated trading where microseconds matter, so systems pin threads to isolated CPUs to avoid scheduling delays.
example: An HFT engine may busy-poll a network card on a dedicated core.

definition: Access by a CPU to memory placed on another NUMA node. It can incur additional interconnect traffic and latency compared with local access; the cost depends on topology and workload.
example: `numactl --hardware` reports local distance 10 and remote distance often around 20.

definition: Under Linux’s usual local policy, a write fault on new private anonymous memory commonly allocates a physical page near the CPU handling it. Explicit policy, cpusets, memory pressure, huge pages and later migration can alter placement.
example: With local policy, enough node-0 memory and no later migration, a main thread on node 0 can place a newly written private array there.

definition: A NUMA policy that distributes page allocations across selected nodes in a repeating pattern. It spreads placement rather than making every thread’s accesses local, and cannot guarantee the elimination of bandwidth hot spots.
example: `numactl --interleave=all ./db` alternates pages between all nodes.

definition: The Linux command for running a program with a chosen NUMA policy (which nodes' CPUs and memory it uses) and for showing the NUMA layout.
example: `numactl --cpunodebind=0 --membind=0 ./db` keeps the database on node 0.

definition: The Linux command that shows how much of a process's (or the system's) memory is on each NUMA node.
example: `numastat -p 1234` shows process 1234's memory per node.

definition: A Linux feature (since 3.8) that periodically unmaps pages to see which node uses them (via "hinting faults"), then moves pages towards their users or tasks towards their memory.
example: `sysctl kernel.numa_balancing=1` turns it on.

definition: A database’s memory cache of database pages, reducing disk reads and buffering changes. Its size and whether processes or threads share it depend on the database and configuration.
example: PostgreSQL's shared_buffers is its buffer pool.

definition: The cgroup v2 file setting CPU bandwidth: "quota period" in microseconds, or "max" for no limit. The group may use quota microseconds of CPU in every period.
example: `echo "200000 100000" > cpu.max` allows 2 CPUs' worth.

definition: A cgroup CPU-time budget shared across its fair-class tasks and CPUs over an accounting period. Exhausted local runtime allocations throttle affected queues. Ancestor budgets, per-CPU accounting and burst credit can change the exact timing; a perfectly simultaneous group-wide stop is an ideal model.
example: A 200 ms quota is spent in 25 ms by 8 busy threads.

definition: The repeating window, 100 ms by default, over which a cgroup's CPU quota is measured and refilled.
example: With a 100 ms period, the quota is replenished ten times a second.

definition: A sharing scheme that never leaves a CPU idle while some group has work. Weights are work-conserving; quotas are not.
example: With weights only, a lone low-weight container can use every idle CPU.

definition: A cgroup v2 setting (Linux 5.14+) that lets a group save unused quota from earlier periods and spend it during short spikes, up to the given amount.
example: With cpu.max.burst set to 50000, a group can briefly use 50 ms more than its quota.

definition: The latency of the slowest requests, such as the worst 1%. Throttling and scheduling delays often hurt the tail much more than the average.
example: A service averaging 5 ms may have a 99th-percentile latency of 80 ms.

definition: A value locating a proportion of a measured distribution: p50 is the median and p99 marks the 99th percentile under the chosen calculation method. P99 describes a high quantile, not the single worst case.
example: A measured p99 of 79 ms marks a high quantile; ties, interpolation and sample size affect how many observations are at or beyond it.

definition: A cgroup v2 CPU-statistics file. With CPU bandwidth control, nr_periods counts enforcement periods and nr_throttled counts those with throttling; their ratio is a period fraction, not CPU utilisation or wall-time loss. throttled_usec measures aggregate throttling and must be interpreted with CPU count and hierarchy in mind.
example: `nr_throttled 9100` out of `nr_periods 36000` means about a quarter of periods throttled.

definition: Real elapsed time, as on a clock on the wall, as opposed to CPU time. Several threads can use more CPU time than wall time.
example: 8 threads running for 25 ms of wall time use 200 ms of CPU time.

definition: A cgroup with no children; its ancestors are the groups above it in the hierarchy. Limits on any ancestor also apply to everything below it.
example: An unlimited leaf inside a parent capped at 2 CPUs is still capped at 2 CPUs.

definition: The Linux command that shows CPU topology: sockets, cores, threads, caches and NUMA nodes. `-e` lists each logical CPU with its core and socket.
example: `lscpu -e` shows which logical CPUs are SMT siblings.

definition: A program using one application thread of execution. Its own instructions cannot execute simultaneously on several CPUs, though libraries, asynchronous devices or kernel work may provide concurrency on its behalf.

Linux’s proportional-share scheduling class for ordinary tasks. Nice values and group weights determine relative CPU service. Classic CFS used smallest virtual runtime; EEVDF instead chooses the earliest virtual deadline among eligible tasks.
The CPU-time budget reserved for a SCHED_DEADLINE task over its period. It should cover the task’s required execution under the stated scheduling assumptions; budget exhaustion can throttle the task.

The allowed time from a job’s release to its required completion. In Linux SCHED_DEADLINE it is supplied separately from CPU runtime and period; admission alone does not prove the application can meet it.
The nominal interval between releases of a repeating SCHED_DEADLINE job and its CPU reservation. A period differs from the relative completion deadline and from a cgroup CPU-quota accounting period.
